This appendix documents a small 2D computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model of a room section. It is used in Part D to show how the placement of an opening, the supply temperature and the airflow decide whether ventilative cooling gives draught at the feet. The model is made for comparing cases and seeing the physics. It does not give design values.
The model exists in two versions that give the same results:
is the reference version in Python, with plotting functions in
and the figures of this appendix in
is the same solver in JavaScript, which runs as the app.

children.value: The room CFD app after a run with the default inputs: a window from 0.9 to 2.1 m, 16 °C supply air and 6 air changes per hour. Open the app to change the inputs.

The app starts a run when it opens. A run simulates 30 minutes of real time and takes under a minute in a browser. The section view shows the instantaneous field while the simulation runs and the time-averaged field when it finishes. Changing a setting starts a new run.

Under Room you can change the depth of the room from the facade (3–10 m) and the ceiling height (2.4–4 m). A third slider moves the 0.4 m wide block of heat gains along the floor. The exhaust slot stays 0.1–0.2 m below the ceiling, and the cells keep the size set under Mesh. The slider beside the colour bar draws one isoline on the section, for example the 0.15 m/s air speed or the 20 % draught rate. Each of the three views keeps its own value.
The app is a single HTML file,
. Save it anywhere and double-click it to use it offline.

The model is a vertical section through a room 5 m deep and 2.5 m high. The room is 4 m wide, which is only used to turn the airflow and the heat gains into values per metre of width. The supply opening sits in the facade at x = 0 and the exhaust is a 0.1 m slot high in the back wall, at 2.3–2.4 m.

The heat gains (people, equipment and sun-heated surfaces lumped together) are a heat source in a block 0.4 m wide and 1.2 m high in the middle of the room. Their size is set so that the well-mixed room temperature is the same in every case:

A steady solver (like SIMPLE in commercial codes) would be faster when the flow has a steady state, but cold air from a window falling into a warm room often flaps and wanders and has none. A time-marching solver handles both cases: it settles if the flow is steady, and it averages if it is not. The fields used for comfort are averaged over the last 10 minutes of the run.
The advection terms decide how much the solution is smeared out. Two schemes are available.

With TVD the speed converges towards about 0.42 m/s, and the default grid is within about 7 % of that. With upwind it keeps rising, because the numerical diffusion shrinks with the cell size. The app uses a coarser grid than Python to keep runs short, so its floor speeds are somewhat lower.
The IEA Annex 20 two-dimensional test case

is an isothermal room 9 m long and 3 m high. Air enters through a 0.168 m slot under the ceiling at 0.455 m/s (a Reynolds number of 5000 based on the slot height) and leaves through a 0.48 m opening at the floor of the opposite wall. Laser-Doppler measurements of the mean velocity are given on two vertical lines (x = H and x = 2H) and two horizontal lines, h/2 below the ceiling and h/2 above the floor. The report and the data are in the book’s
runs the case on a 321 × 107 grid.

compares a normal window (sill at 0.9 m, head at 2.1 m) with a top hatch (2.2–2.4 m), both fully open, at 6 air changes per hour. The gains are set for a well-mixed room at 26 °C, and the supply air is 10 K colder, at 16 °C, as on a summer night.

From the window the cold air falls 0.9 m along the facade and runs along the floor. It slows down about 1 m into the room but leaves a cool layer of about 22 °C over the floor (
The flow from the top hatch does not stay on the ceiling. The opening is low and narrow, so the inflow is fast and the Archimedes number is large (

), and the jet falls along the facade from 2.2 m. It gains more speed on the way down than the window flow and reaches the floor at up to 0.39 m/s against 0.29 m/s. The fast floor stream also reaches further into the room: the ISO 7730 draught rate is above 20 % up to about 1.6 m from the facade, against about 0.9 m for the window. The air at the floor is 1.5–2 K warmer than with the window, because the falling jet mixes with room air on its way down.

Neither opening meets ISO 7730 near the facade at this supply temperature, while both stay below the ASHRAE 55 ankle limit, at 15 % for the window and 17 % for the hatch. The hatch in the model is a plain slot in the wall. A real bottom-hung hatch deflects the inflow upwards, which helps it attach to the ceiling (
), so the result is a worst case for the hatch.
